content: Pyrimethamine works through pharmacodynamic synergism. Its minor significance is unknown, but it can increase bone marrow toxicity, necessitating close monitoring. Quinidine increases the levels or effects of sulfamethoxazole by competing for renal tubular clearance of basic (cationic) drugs. This interaction is serious, as both quinidine and sulfamethoxazole prolong the QTc interval. Alternative drugs should be used. Additionally, sulfamethoxazole increases quinine levels through the same mechanism, though the significance of this interaction is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole increases ramelteon levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism, though the clinical significance is unknown. Close monitoring is advised. Similarly, sulfamethoxazole and ranolazine both prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution and close monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole increases repaglinide levels by competing for plasma protein binding, necessitating caution and monitoring. Rifampin and rifapentine decrease sulfamethoxazole levels by inducing CYP2C9/10 metabolism, though the significance is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole and risperidone both prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution and monitoring. Non-aspirin salicylates, salsalate, and selegiline transdermal increase sulfamethoxazole levels through unspecified mechanisms, though the significance is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole increases siponimod levels by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism. This interaction is serious, and alternative drugs should be used. Co-administration of siponimod with moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitors is not recommended, and caution is advised with moderate CYP2C9 inhibitors alone. Sulfamethoxazole decreases the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism. Antibiotics reduce the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by disrupting colonic bacterial flora needed for drug activation. This interaction is serious, and alternative drugs should be used. Sulfamethoxazole and sotalol both prolong the QTc interval, requiring alternative drugs. Spironolactone increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism, though the significance is unclear. Sulfasalazine also increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. Sulfamethoxazole affects tamoxifen metabolism by inhibiting CYP2C9/10, reducing the formation of active metabolites. Close monitoring is required. Sulfamethoxazole and telavancin both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating caution and monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole increases terbinafine levels by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism, requiring caution and monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole decreases thiamine levels by altering intestinal flora, but this applies only to oral forms of both agents. The significance is unclear. Thioridazine and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Ticlopidine increases sulfamethoxazole levels by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism, though the significance is unclear. Torasemide increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism, though the significance is unclear. Tranylcypromine also increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. Sulfamethoxazole and trazodone both prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution and monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole decreases trazodone levels through an unspecified mechanism, though the significance is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole and tretinoin (oral or topical) increase phototoxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is serious, and alternative drugs should be used. Sulfamethoxazole increases triamterene levels by competing for renal tubular clearance of basic (cationic) drugs. Triamterene also increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism, though the significance is unclear. Trifluoperazine and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating close monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole increases trimethoprim levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. Trimipramine and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval, requiring close monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole decreases trimipramine levels through an unspecified mechanism, though the significance is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole and tropisetron both prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution and monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole decreases the effects of the live typhoid vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction is contraindicated, and live bacterial vaccines should be administered only after completing antibiotic therapy. Valganciclovir increases sulfamethoxazole toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, though the significance is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole and valoctocogene roxaparvovec may both increase hepatotoxicity, requiring close monitoring and consideration of alternative medications. Valproic acid increases sulfamethoxazole levels by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism, though the significance is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole and venlafaxine both prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution and monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole increases verapamil levels by competing for renal tubular clearance of basic (cationic) drugs, though the significance is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole and verteporfin increase phototoxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Sulfamethoxazole and voriconazole both prolong the QTc interval, requiring close monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole increases voriconazole levels by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism, and voriconazole increases sulfamethoxazole levels through the same mechanism. Sulfamethoxazole increases warfarin levels by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism and displacing protein binding. Therapy modification and close monitoring are required, with a potential warfarin dose reduction of 10–20%. Willow bark increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism, though the significance is unclear. Zafirlukast increases sulfamethoxazole levels by inhibiting CYP2C9/10 metabolism, though the significance is unclear. Zidovudine increases sulfamethoxazole toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, while sulfamethoxazole increases zidovudine levels by reducing renal clearance. The significance is unclear, but close monitoring is advised. Sulfamethoxazole and ziprasidone both prolong the QTc interval, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring.
